primary_claim: Evaluation Conditioned Training (ECT), which augments training data with evaluation labels describing how a sample will be evaluated and varies those labels at deployment, reduces political bias by 53.9% versus SFT baseline and reduces sycophancy on addition problems versus PPO baselines, in proof-of-concept experiments.

effect.metric: bias score reduction / sycophancy false-positive rate
effect.value: 53.9% reduction in bias score vs SFT baseline (outperforms in 85% of 200 test topics), 41.8% improvement vs shuffled baseline; sycophancy decreased vs shuffled and PPO baselines on addition problems

stated_future_work: Apply ECT to coding solutions, where models of varying sizes or thinking budgets act as monitors for accuracy
Test if an RL setup can be made as robust as the bias setting
Replicate results on more realistic tasks with more nuanced grading
Continue exploring training procedures that prevent degenerate solutions that ignore or mis-generalize the labeling channel
limitations_stated: 4-bit quantization and 3B/7B model sizes were likely meaningful limitations
Sycophancy setting was highly dependent on several interventions (entropy bonus, hyperparameter tuning) unlike the more robust bias setting
Uncertain as to the cause of a slight uptick in sycophancy around 0% suggestibility
Central open challenge: how far this generalizes, especially to realistic human and model-judge monitoring regimes
quote: ECT achieves a 53.9% reduction in bias scores compared to the SFT baseline, with a near-universal improvement across test cases.
